component.name: oxidom
component.summary: Xray client for the GNOME desktop

description.p: oxidom ("oxided freedom") is a native Xray / v2ray client. It manages subscriptions and servers, runs the Xray core for you, and routes traffic through a local proxy with an optional system-proxy toggle.
Supports VLESS (including Reality), VMess, Trojan and Shadowsocks servers, subscription formats from common panels, country flags, latency checks and latency sorting.

Servers are no longer only what a provider sends. One can be typed in field by field, edited in place without losing its alias or its pinned certificate — and on a subscription, an edit survives every refresh, with the card marking what was overridden and offering to take the provider's value back. The expanded card lists every parameter the server carries, credentials masked until revealed, and handing a server to somebody else as a share-link now names what the link cannot carry instead of passing on a server that works for one person and not the other.

The Xray core is managed: the tested release is downloaded into oxidom's own data directory on first use and verified against a digest pinned in its source, so nothing has to be installed by hand. XHTTP and gRPC nodes keep the transport settings their links specify, a latency check started before a reconnect no longer paints a healthy tunnel as failed, the log view neither repeats lines written during an operation nor loses the app's own lines to a daemon restart, and a session shut down cleanly is no longer remembered as running when nothing listens on its ports.

A fixes-only release. The most important one closes a window in which traffic could leave outside the tunnel: while the application was automatically reconnecting a tunnel whose core had died, it briefly removed the routes that were holding traffic back. Reconnection now keeps those routes installed until the new connection stands.

Beyond that: a failed connection attempt no longer cancels an ongoing automatic reconnect or leaves a stale latency reading on the card; proxy passwords with special characters, half-filled proxy credentials, IPv6 share links, HTTP-camouflaged servers and Clash imports that use HTTP camouflage all work as their sources intended; and several small interface wrongs — a Connect button that first disconnected a dead group, a banner counting dead sessions, a chart line repeating the failure stated under it, blank toasts — say the right thing now.

This release is about the interface telling the truth about what it did. The expanded server card draws the record behind its number as a chart instead of ten lines of text: a column per check, oldest at the left, with a failed check marked apart from a slot no check has filled and the range stated beside the heading. Its right-click menu covers the whole card rather than only the strip at the top, and the reason a check produced no number sits under the chart with its two actions as icons.

A problem report no longer names the provider. Server names, aliases and the tags built from them are taken out along with addresses, host names and credentials; each distinct value carries its own numbered mark, so one host can be followed through a report without being readable; and the footer names every mark the report can contain and says what was kept on purpose.

A pool's health check is a setting rather than one hard-coded address, for the machine or for one profile, and a pool that carried no traffic says whether that check ever succeeded instead of only counting nodes. Stopping a latency sweep says how many checks it stopped, and a stop is offered only where one lands. A paste lands in the field it was aimed at. Connecting a group of servers names the session it runs in. Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora users can install oxidom with one command from the README.

This release is about the application accounting for itself. An About dialog names the versions of the interface, the daemon and the Xray core, and says so plainly when they disagree. A failed latency check now states its reason on the card, how the check was actually made and how long ago, and the card lists the recent checks rather than the newest number alone.

A problem report can be assembled from the log page with addresses, host names, account ids and credentials taken out and marked where they stood, so a log can be attached to a bug report without being read line by line first.

A latency check can be called off. A profile can carry its own routing rules. The source of the geo data is a setting. Connecting a group of servers saves nothing and rewrites nothing. The server grid opens at the width it has instead of one column, and a wide window carries a fourth column. A tunnel whose core dies holds its traffic instead of releasing it unprotected. oxidom is also installable from a signed package repository.
The first release. oxidom manages subscriptions and servers, runs an Xray core for you, and exposes the tunnel as local SOCKS5 and HTTP proxies, with an optional GNOME system-proxy toggle.

Browse servers as a card grid with country flags and latency sorting, keep several tunnels running side by side, balance across a pool of servers so one dead node does not end the session, and send a single command through a profile without touching anything else.
The interface needs no privileges of its own, and oxidom never escalates: the only privileged part is an optional system daemon, used for network interfaces.
